The Auditor and Note by Note
Take Three Kinds of Qualification Seriously
A provision set below what’s needed (tax, doubtful receivables)
Stagnant receivables from related parties
Doubt about going concern
An item that repeats and grows for several years means management has no intention of fixing it.
Also read the auditor’s “other legal responsibilities” section (Article 129 transactions, compliance with exchange rules).
Note by Note
What to check
Inventory
Valuation method (average or FIFO; LIFO isn’t allowed under the Iranian standard, please check), holding period
Growing faster than sales; reversing write-downs to lift profit
Receivables
Age of receivables, related parties’ share, provision
A lengthening collection period, a smaller provision
Provisions
The tax provision against the assessment and the final ruling
Reversing provisions for profit; a big gap with the assessment
Fixed assets
Depreciation method and life, finance costs in the asset’s cost
A multi-year project “under construction” whose finance costs go into the asset; a longer useful life
Currency
Translation rate (the available rate; please check), currency position
A large non-recurring translation gain; export receivables not repatriated

Buying and selling prices with the group, balances
Sales below market; a growing balance owed by the parent
Contracting revenue
Percentage of completion
Contract receivables growing faster than revenue

Correcting errors or changing policy

Match each note to its red flag.
Reversing write-downs to lift profit
Finance costs of a multi-year project added to the asset
Each note has its own way of making profit look bigger.
A qualification about the tax provision has repeated three years in a row and grown each year. Meaning?
Management has no intention of fixing it; the real profit is lower
The problem is being solved and the provision is enough
It doesn’t matter because it concerns past years’ tax
A repeated, growing qualification is a red flag.
A project has been “under construction” for five years and its finance costs are added to the asset’s cost. The effect?
Finance costs stay out of the income statement and profit looks bigger
Profit looks smaller because finance costs are recorded twice
No effect; finance costs only show in the cash flow
Capitalising the finance costs of an endless project makes profit look bigger.
Large or repeated prior-year adjustments mean past years’ reported profit wasn’t right.
See it in the statement of changes in equity.
What does lengthening the useful life of assets do to profit?
Depreciation falls and profit rises
Depreciation rises and profit falls
Only cash flow changes, not profit
Changing the depreciation method or life is one of the signs of earnings management.
Hidden Inflation and Accruals
Two Inflation Effects Hidden in Profit

Inventory gains: under the average method, goods made more cheaply are sold at today’s price. The margin looks better than it is, and this part doesn’t become free cash (the inventory must be replaced at the new price).
Cheap depreciation: fixed assets are at historical cost. The note on “insurance cover of assets” shows an approximate replacement value (check that the company has this note).
The Accruals Ratio
Company D: (830,000 − 900,000) ÷ 4,275,000 = minus 1.6%; cash above profit; good.
Company E: profit 1,000, cash 200, assets 5,000 → 16%; most of the profit hasn’t turned into cash.
With high inflation this ratio is usually positive in Iran; compare it with peers and past years. If it is above about 10% two years in a row and above peers, find the cause.
Accruals = (net profit − operating cash flow) ÷ average total assets
Seven Signs of Earnings Management
Profit grows and operating cash flow doesn’t, two years in a row
A large non-operating gain in the last quarter, when the year’s forecast wasn’t met
Reversing provisions or cutting the receivables provision in a weak year
Changing the depreciation method, useful life or inventory valuation
Repeated prior-year adjustments
Late publication or a sudden change of auditor
High accounting profit, a low dividend and growing borrowing
Net profit 1,000, operating cash flow 200, average assets 5,000. The accruals ratio?
(1,000 − 200) ÷ 5,000 = 16%; most of the profit hasn’t turned into cash yet.
Profit 830,000, operating cash flow 900,000, average assets 4,275,000. The accruals ratio? (a negative with a minus sign)
What do you compare the accruals ratio with?
Peers and the same company’s past years
A fixed global number, say 10%
Companies in completely different industries
With high inflation this ratio is usually positive.
Which items are signs of earnings management?
Sign of earnings management
Normal
A large asset-sale gain in the last quarter when the forecast wasn’t met
Cutting the receivables provision in a weak operating year
A sudden change of auditor
Operating cash flow keeping pace with profit
The same depreciation method for 10 years
Memorise the seven signs.
Why don’t “inventory gains” turn into free cash under inflation?
Because the inventory sold must be replaced at the new, higher price
Because inventory gains aren’t taxed and don’t appear in net profit
Because inventory isn’t recorded on the balance sheet at all
Part of the high margin goes into buying inventory again.
Which note shows the approximate replacement value of assets?
Insurance cover of assets
Other non-operating income
Retained earnings and reserves
Its gap with book value is the size of the cheap-depreciation effect.
Explain why a company whose profit grows but whose operating cash flow doesn’t should be checked carefully.

It means profit is recorded but hasn’t turned into cash, and accruals are high. Receivables or inventory may be piling up, or earnings management may be at work. A low CFO-to-profit ratio means low profit quality.
Profit hasn’t turned into cash; high accruals
Receivables or inventory may be piling up, or there may be earnings management
A low CFO/NI means low profit quality
Two years in a row of this pattern is one of the seven signs of earnings management.
ROIC and Competitive Advantage
Return on Capital
Capital employed = net fixed assets + trade receivables + inventory − trade payables.

In Iran the denominator is at historical cost, so nominal ROIC is overstated. Read it over 5 years and next to peers. To compare with WACC, make both real or replace fixed assets with their insurance cover.
Growth creates value only when the return on new capital exceeds its cost.
ROIC = NOPAT ÷ capital employed\nIncremental ROIC = change in NOPAT ÷ change in capital employed (3 to 5 years, constant prices)

The Durability Test
Don’t treat a policy advantage as permanent; build a scenario for losing it.
A low-volatility 5-year gross margin and ROIC above peers in most years = a real advantage.
A high margin only in a currency-jump year isn’t an advantage; it’s the cycle.
NOPAT 300 and capital employed 1,500. ROIC?
1,000 was invested over 5 years and real NOPAT rose by 180. Incremental ROIC?
180 ÷ 1,000 = 18%; above the real WACC of 8% → value created.
Company B also reports “profit growth”, but its incremental ROIC is 4% and the real WACC is 8%. Conclusion?
Its growth destroyed value
It created value because profit grew
No effect
Profit growth is not the same as creating value.
Match each advantage to what breaks it.
A change in regulation
A cost advantage from its own mine
A change in government mining royalties
A policy advantage is the most fragile.
A high nominal ROIC at an Iranian company alone shows the business is excellent.
The denominator is at historical cost and nominal ROIC is overstated.
A sign of a real, durable advantage?
A low-volatility 5-year gross margin and ROIC above peers in most years
A very high margin in a dollar-jump year and record sales profit, above all peers
Cheap subsidised feedstock set by government decision
One good year is the cycle, not an advantage.
Capital Allocation, Management and the Quality Scorecard
Where Does the Cash Go?
Add up 5 years of CFO: maintenance CAPEX, expansion projects, dividends, debt repayment, treasury shares (check the rules), buying other companies’ shares.
Did previous projects finish on time and on budget?
Was the return promised in the justification report achieved?
Does the payout ratio fit the company’s investment needs or the major shareholder’s cash needs?
Is the company’s cash kept with the parent company?

The Quality Scorecard (0 to 2 per line)

5-year ROIC against peers • real incremental ROIC against WACC • gross margin stability • 5-year CFO/NI (under 0.7 / 0.7 to 0.9 / 0.9+) • source of advantage (policy only / mixed / non-policy) • debt (over 3× EBITDA / 1 to 3 / under 1) • project record • audit and disclosure.
12 to 16 high quality; 8 to 11 medium; below 8 only if very cheap, with caution.
The scorecard is not a buy signal; it tells you how far to trust the valuation number and what margin of safety to demand.
A company’s scorecard points: 2, 1, 2, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2. Total?
A total of 13 → high quality (12 to 16).
The scorecard total is 7. Meaning?
Only if it’s very cheap, and even then with caution
High quality; suitable for a large portfolio weight
A signal to buy immediately with all your money
Below 8 means little trust in the value number.
What does the quality scorecard NOT do?
It doesn’t give a buy signal or replace valuation
It doesn’t show how far to trust the value number
It doesn’t tell you the margin of safety needed
A good company at an expensive price is also a bad investment.
Where do you best judge management from?
The Codal record: past interpretive reports, publication timing, dividend payments
The CEO’s TV interviews and speeches
The number of followers on the company’s channel and page
The record, not the talk.
The 5-year average CFO/NI is 0.8. The score for this line?
0.7 to 0.9 → 1 point.
A capital increase from revaluation brings the company cash.
It’s usually to fix the financial structure or get out of Article 141.
The company’s balance owed by its parent grows every year. What does it mean for capital allocation?
The company’s cash is kept with the parent; worrying
Excellent group-level liquidity management and lower finance costs for the company
More profit from deposit interest held with the parent
Retail shareholders’ money is in the major shareholder’s hands.
